title: Maritime Relay Framework for Networks: Resilient Backup Routing for Global Internet Traffic During Subsea and Orbital Outages
content: Submarine fiber-optic cables carry the majority of intercontinental data traffic followed by Satellite Internet. Lately, in 2026 reported Iranian threats against the cables in the Strait of Hormuz made this vulnerability more alarming. This paper proposes a satellite and cable independent backup layer using maritime traffic in which commercial vessels become relay nodes as a Vessel-borne Delay-Tolerant Network (VDTN) and the sea tier of a Space-Air-Ground-Sea Integrated Network (SAGSIN). When the normal medium is unavailable or jeopardized, Marine ships forward short critical messages hop by hop over short-range and long-range radios, about approx. 50km apart, using a compact protocol proposed in this paper, C-Communication, and can also carry bulk data physically between ports. a link- budget, channel-capacity, and hop analysis for the Europe-to-Far East Marine routes; (ii) a backup ship-tracking service with witness-based detection and identification of gray shipping; (iii) an additional feature as a tip-and-cue interface to establish backup to orbital compute that survives loss of the orbital tier; (iv) a reward scheme in which participating ships are paid in port-fee credits or, optionally,cryptocurrency; and (v) a security design and a staged evaluation plan. Delay in repairs to both submarine cables and Satellite links is hours to days, so this proposed layer suits tracking, alerts, and critical messages (real-time services may not be included initially). It is a resilience layer, not a replacement for broadband satellite or cable capacity, and orbital compute is an optional accelerator, not a full stack dependency.
